title: Investors pouring money into malls
full_text:
Retail property is locking in its position as the most active sector this half, with players lining up assets ranging from fund houses MA Financial and HMC Capital, to major superannuation funds looking to expand.
They are betting they can defy the cost-of-living crisis and the negative wealth effect from the housing slump, with Scentre Group, owner of the local Westfield empire, saying it was not seeing an impact on its business.
In the latest transactions, MA Financial has added two shopping centres to its holdings, and has flagged it will push into the large-format retail sector It is buying Taigum Square in Brisbane from Vicinity Centres for $120m, and has carved off the ECQ XL large-format retail centre from a larger property Vicinity recently bought in western Sydney. MA Financial is paying close to $70m for the asset.
MA Financial joint chief executive Julian Biggins is bullish about the prospects of the retail sector after the company acquired $1.2bn of shopping centres last year.
“We currently have over $500m of retail shopping centre transactions that we’re starting to raise capital for, which we expect to contribute significantly to the second half net flows,” he said.
The deals are being handled by CBRE head of retail capital markets Simon Rooney, who is upbeat on the sector.
“The transactions highlight the sustained demand for high-quality retail real estate investment opportunities,” Mr Rooney said.
MA Financial is not alone in seeking to expand, with David Di Pilla’s HMC Capital flagging that its retail property funds had around $2bn of firepower at their disposal to make acquisitions.
Other large institutions have also been active, with superannuation giant Australian Retirement Trust getting clearance for its deal to buy a 50 per cent interest in Westfield Mount Gravatt in Brisbane.
The super fund giant will pay Scentre $882.5m for a half share in the complex after getting approval from the Australian Competition and Consumer Competition clearance.
Scentre has already sold interests in a series of shopping centres, bringing in investors to refresh it balance sheet after it avoided raising discounted capital during the pandemic. The company is now bolstering its capital structure by refinancing expensive debt and introducing joint-venture capital while keeping control of the assets.
The latest investment in Westfield Mt Gravatt shopping centre follows ART’s $864m acquisition of a 19.9 per cent interest in Westfield Sydney in February. ART’s general manager Mid Risk Assets, Michael Weaver, said Westfield Mt Gravatt attracted millions of shoppers and offered development potential.
Scentre told investors it was continuing to receive inbound interest in its premium portfolio, with chief executive Elliott Rusanow saying retail property is attracting more capital.
“I think based on the volume of inbound inquiries and meeting requests, that potential capital partners want to meet with us and become future partners of Scentre Group.
“I would say that it’s not slowing down at all. If anything, the demand is growing even further,” he said. The largest collection of assets currently on the market is the Jen Retail Portfolio, which is expected to attract bids of more than $1bn. The sale process starts in early September.
